lead_headline: Arvada Council Reviews Streamlined Two-Page Strategic Plan

type_specific.meeting_summary: The Arvada City Council reviewed a proposed two-page revision of the city's 2024–2030 Strategic Plan, which staff condensed from a 25-page document into a one-page vision sheet and one-page operational strategy. Council members offered feedback on visual prioritization, accountability mechanisms, community engagement, and how the plan should connect to day-to-day project decisions. No vote was taken; staff will collect council input and bring a finalized version forward for approval by resolution this fall, with an effective date of January 1, 2027.

prose_paragraphs: Staff presented a proposed overhaul of the city's 2024–2030 Strategic Plan, reducing it from a 25-page document to two pages. The redesign was prompted by direction council gave at an April 18 strategic planning retreat, where members described the existing plan as too complicated, hard to engage with, and more operational than strategic. Staff worked with the leadership team over several months to produce the new format, which retains all content from the old plan but reorganizes and simplifies it. The first page, titled 'Future Ready Arvada,' presents five strategic results in the priority order council established in April — Physical and Technology Systems, Local Economy, Quality of Life, Homelessness, and Housing — each described in three plain-language visionary statements. Guiding principles drawn from a January team-building retreat appear at the bottom of that page.

The second page, described as the 'operational strategy,' consolidates what had been numerous overlapping goals under each priority area into four overarching strategic goals per category. For example, eight goals previously listed under Local Economy were merged into four broader statements. Staff emphasized that no new content was introduced — all language traces directly to the existing plan. The presenter also noted that a publicly accessible infrastructure dashboard is already live on the city's website, tracking progress toward paving 75 lane miles by year-end, and cited this as a model for future reporting tied to the strategic plan. Staff indicated they intend to develop additional dashboards and reporting tools covering permitting and customer service, grants, safety, and climate action.

Council members raised several substantive concerns about implementation. Multiple members noted that the visual layout of the vision page does not clearly communicate that the five priority areas are ranked, and suggested graphic adjustments. Mayor Pro Tem Moorman proposed changing the Quality of Life statement 'ensure a safe community' to 'ensure a safe and resilient community,' partly to reflect the city's adopted Climate Action and Sustainability Plan (CASP); other council members suggested 'resilient' alone was broad enough to encompass climate, risk mitigation, and other concerns. Council members also pressed staff on how individual projects would be traceable to specific strategic goals — a 'golden thread' — and how the plan would factor into performance evaluations of city appointees. Staff acknowledged that the alignment and reporting framework is still being developed and committed to iterative updates through 2027. The plan is expected to be approved by resolution this fall and take effect January 1, 2027.

questions_raised: Councilmember Griffith asked whether the visual design of the vision page should more clearly reflect the ranked priority order of the five strategic results.

Mayor Pro Tem Moorman suggested adding 'resilient' to the Quality of Life 'safe community' statement to incorporate climate and risk concerns, and asked whether the climate-related language in the operational strategy was sufficient.

Mayor Pro Tem Moorman asked how council and staff can be confident that individual projects are genuinely and directly connected to the strategic goals — avoiding the loose 'golden thread' problem seen in the old plan.

Councilmember Lovisone asked how the plan connects to the city's existing WIG (Wildly Important Goal) framework and whether each priority area should have its own WIG or whether multiple WIGs can share a lane.
Councilmember Lovisone asked where and how council will evaluate whether the plan is being implemented, beyond workshop report-outs.
Councilmember Lovisone asked whether alignment with the strategic plan should be incorporated into performance feedback and growth plans for council's appointees.

Councilmember Fifer suggested the plan be used as a scoring or filtering tool to evaluate whether proposed new projects should be undertaken at all, and asked if staff could develop a multi-criteria alignment score for projects.
Councilmember Ambrose asked whether there is a defined process for a 'parking lot' of future strategic priorities, and how the plan will guide decisions between competing interests.
Councilmember Simpson asked whether the strategic plan would be used in public engagement efforts and how residents could see how city actions connect back to the plan's commitments.
An unidentified council member asked about the 'delayed up to 30 days' language on the infrastructure dashboard and whether it would confuse the public into thinking work is behind schedule.
